facts.value: Overtime after 8 hours/day AND after 40 hours/week
facts.summary: Alaska requires 1.5x pay for hours over 8 in a day, in addition to hours over 40 in a week, which is stricter than the federal FLSA (weekly-only) standard.
facts.sourceAgency: Alaska Department of Labor and Workforce Development, Wage and Hour Administration
facts.notes: Daily and weekly OT hours are not double-counted. Certain categorical exemptions apply, including employers with fewer than 4 employees (AS 23.10.060).

facts.value: 2x state minimum wage for a 40-hour week (approx $1,120/week at the $14.00 minimum wage effective July 1, 2026)
facts.summary: Alaska's white-collar (executive/administrative/professional) exemption requires a salary of at least two times the state minimum wage for the first 40 hours, a higher floor than the federal $684/week salary level.
facts.sourceAgency: Alaska Department of Labor and Workforce Development, Wage and Hour Administration
facts.notes: Threshold floats with the state minimum wage (2x minimum wage x 40 hrs). At $14.00/hr this equals roughly $1,120/week. Verify the exact current weekly figure with Wage and Hour, as the base minimum wage adjusts annually beginning Jan 1, 2028.

facts.summary: Alaska's minimum wage is $14.00 per hour effective July 1, 2026, well above the federal $7.25; tip credits are not allowed.
facts.sourceAgency: Alaska Department of Labor and Workforce Development, Wage and Hour Administration
facts.notes: Scheduled to rise to $15.00 on July 1, 2027, then annual inflation adjustments starting Jan 1, 2028 (2024 Ballot Measure 1). Alaska prohibits a tip credit, so there is no separate tipped wage.

facts.summary: Beyond the federal categories, Alaska law also prohibits employment discrimination based on marital status, changes in marital status, pregnancy, parenthood, sexual orientation, and gender identity or expression.
facts.sourceAgency: Alaska State Commission for Human Rights
facts.notes: Alaska also covers the federal classes (race, color, religion, sex, national origin, age, disability). Listed here are additions relative to the federal baseline.

facts.summary: Alaska's anti-discrimination law applies to employers with at least one employee, far below the federal 15-employee threshold under Title VII/ADA.
facts.sourceAgency: Alaska State Commission for Human Rights
facts.notes: Commission's Quick Facts for Employers states that having at least one employee brings an employer under AS 18.80.220.

facts.summary: A discrimination complaint must be filed with the Alaska State Commission for Human Rights within 300 days of the alleged discriminatory act.
facts.sourceAgency: Alaska State Commission for Human Rights
facts.notes: Commission's official page: complaint must be drafted, notarized, and filed within 300 days of the alleged act.

facts.value: 2 years (unpaid overtime/minimum wage); 3 years (straight-time or promised wages/benefits)
facts.summary: Claims for unpaid overtime or minimum wage must be brought within two years, while straight-time wage or promised-benefit claims have a longer limitations period.
facts.sourceAgency: Alaska Department of Labor and Workforce Development, Wage and Hour Administration
facts.notes: AS 23.10.130 sets a 2-year limit for minimum wage/overtime/liquidated damages actions. The 3-year figure for straight-time/promised wages reflects the general contract limitations period as stated in the DOL FAQ; verify the applicable period for a specific claim type.

facts.value: Within 3 working days of employer termination; next regular payday (at least 3 days after notice) if employee quits
facts.summary: When an employer terminates an employee, all wages are due within three working days; when an employee quits, wages are due on the next regular payday at least three days after notice.
facts.sourceAgency: Alaska Department of Labor and Workforce Development, Wage and Hour Administration
facts.notes: Working days exclude weekends and legal holidays. Late payment may trigger a penalty of the employee's regular wage from demand until payment, up to a maximum of 90 working days.

facts.value: Public employees protected under the Alaska Whistleblower Act; safety-complaint retaliation protection under AKOSH
facts.summary: Alaska's Whistleblower Act protects public employees who report matters of public concern, and AKOSH protects employees from retaliation for raising occupational safety and health complaints.
facts.sourceAgency: Alaska Department of Labor and Workforce Development (AKOSH); Alaska State Legislature
facts.notes: The Alaska Whistleblower Act (AS 39.90.100) applies to public employers/employees. Private-sector employees also have anti-retaliation protection for filing discrimination complaints (AS 18.80.220) and for occupational safety complaints (AKOSH). Verify statute cite for the specific retaliation context.
